articles.title: Tiger Woods Gives Injury Update, Returns to Driving Range in New Video
articles.summary: Tiger Woods hasn't made a start on the PGA Tour in over two years, but he appears to be inching closer to a return.
articles.body:
Tiger Woods hasn't made a start on the PGA Tour in over two years, but he appears to be inching closer to a return.

Before this weekend's Biltmore Championship in Asheville, North Carolina, Woods was seen on the driving range, showing his progress in his recovery from injuries suffered in a car accident earlier this year.

"I can hit pretty much anything," Woods said when asked where he is in his recovery. "I'm a little stiff today because, obviously, last night we were all hanging out, having fun."

Woods announced in March that he would be taking some time away from golf to focus on getting healthy.

"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritize my well-being and work toward lasting recovery," he said at the time . "I'm committed to taking the time needed to return to a healthier, stronger, and more focused place, both personally and professionally."

A 15-time major champion, Woods has not won on the PGA Tour since the 2019 ZOZO Championship, which marked his 82nd career victory to tie Sam Snead's all-time record. He previously said that he has had seven back surgeries and over 20 operations on his leg.

At 50 years old, Woods doesn't have anything left to prove in the sport of golf. Still, it looks like he's motivated to get back to the game he loves, and Tuesday's appearance on the driving range seems to be a step in the right direction.

articles.title: PGA Tour's new structure, plans for 2028 don't include LIV players
articles.summary: The PGA Tour mapped out its new two-tier system that will be incorporated for the 2028 season.
articles.body:
The PGA Tour's future form is coming into focus, and it doesn't currently include a path back for LIV Golf players.

Tuesday morning, PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp announced that the Tour has finalized the qualification models for its impending two-track system, set to start in 2028, and has established the ways that players can move between the upper-tier Championship Series and lower-tier Challenger Series.

"We set out to preserve the meritocracy of our sport and build a competitive model that rewards excellence and ensures a clear path for top performers at each stage of their career," Rolapp said, adding that the "new eligibility structure … will do just that."

At the same time, Rolapp briefly addressed the elephant in the room — and announced that there was no room for it. With LIV Golf currently in dire financial straits and its players uncertain of their future, Rolapp made it clear that the PGA Tour will not be offering a lifeboat, or any kind of return opportunity like the one Brooks Koepka used earlier this year.

"We are not currently contemplating a returning-member program like the one you saw in January," Rolapp said. "Everyone at the PGA Tour, myself included, has been focused on what is best for the organization," he said, adding that the Tour's goal now is "building the optimal competitive model for the future."

Explaining the Tour's two-tier structure

That future will include two tiers of competition, with the opportunity to move between the two depending on performance. The 2027 season will be used to set the fields, which will begin starting in the 2028 season.

Once it's fully underway, the Championship Series will include players meeting a number of criteria, including the top 90 players from the previous season, the top 20 players from the previous year's Challenger Series, and two-time winners on the previous season's Challenger Series. Winners of any Championship Series event or major in previous years win a two-year exemption.

Players on the Challenger Series and new to the PGA Tour can play their way onto the Championship Series through several pathways and a "last chance" series. Challenger Series participants can qualify through PGA Tour University, the Korn Ferry Tour, Q School, or by winning a major within the last four years, among other pathways. A fall "last chance" series will offer three slots on the Championship Series.

For the 2027 season, players will be able to set themselves up for the incoming two-track format by winning tournaments, with each tournament format — major/signature events, full-field events, and opposite-field events — offering differing lengths of exemption for the 2028 season and beyond.

While the specifics of both series' qualifications are primarily relevant only to the players and their interested parties, the overall motivation is obvious: play good golf to get on the Challenger Series, play great golf to get on the Championship Series.

The Tour also announced the points system for the Championship Series, with the goal of rewarding both winners and strong finishers while at the same time giving value to making the cut. Players will effectively compete against one another for points, theoretically making it easier for fans to determine who's playing well over the course of a full season and who's in danger of falling out of the top-tier series.

The winner of a given tournament will receive 300 points, with second and third place receiving 200 and 150, respectively. The 65th-place finisher will receive 30 points, and no finish below that will earn points. As with exemptions, this will likely be easier to grasp in practice than on a spreadsheet.

articles.title: Solheim Cup: England Golf makes fresh call for government support to bring 2030 edition to England for first time
articles.summary: Team Europe regained the Solheim Cup with victory over Team USA in the Netherlands; no venue has been announced for the next edition on European soil in 2030; England not among the seven previous European countries have hosted Solheim Cups
articles.body:
The Solheim Cup has been held in seven different European countries but never in England, but the venue for the 2030 contest - the next edition on European soil - has yet to be finalised.

Multiple venues have expressed interest in hosting, including The Grove in Hertfordshire, although government funding would be required - without private investment - to support any application to bring the event to England.

Discussions continue over the next European venue, with England Golf CEO Jeremy Tomlinson confident that bringing the biennial contest would offer 'immeasurable good' for the sport.

"The Solheim Cup is in a really good place and it's going to get bigger," Tomlinson told Sky Sports . "I honestly think if we bring the Solheim Cup to England we can double, maybe even treble the crowds.

"We have several clubs that really want to put themselves forward and would really like to host the event. With a bit of government help, we really believe that we could bring it to England and it should be here for the first time.

"We're working with clubs, we're working with IMG and the Ladies European Tour and we have talks ongoing with UK Sport. I don't want to say too much, but we're feeling really positive about things and we would love to be able to bring it to England."

The cost to stage a Solheim Cup is less than a tenth of the money required for a Ryder Cup, the equivalent event in the men's game, with Tomlinson hoping the government can underwrite any bid and help create a historic event on English soil.

"It always easy when you perhaps have an entrepreneur that comes forward and can underwrite a whole event, but we haven't had that yet," Tomlinson added.

"We are somewhat dependent upon government to be able to step forward and help us. We have some discussions with them right now and they are positive, they are constructive.

"It a lot of money that you need to be able to put this on, but we truly believe - and I think government feel it as well - that the returns from a feel-good factor and a promotion of an incredible sport could be dynamic."

Team Europe regained the Solheim Cup with an impressive 15-13 victory at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands on Sunday, where a packed grandstand welcomed players onto the first tee and three of Anna Nordqvist's winning side were from England.

"Golf has continued to boom since the pandemic, there is no two ways about that," Tomlinson explained. "We have in excess of 12 and a half million people just in England, who in some way, shape or form, touch golf or participate in golf.

"We have an incredible amount of women that enjoy playing golf away from golf courses. We'd love more women, more girls to be able to come to the golf courses, but they need to have heroes and they need to have people to inspire them.

"We at England Golf truly believe that if we could get the Solheim Cup, it could do immeasurable good for the game of golf and for women in sport. It would be a very, very proud moment."

Sky Sports News has contacted the Department of Media, Culture and Sport for comment.

The next edition of the Solheim Cup will be in 2028 and take place at Valhalla Golf Club in Kentucky from September 8-10 that year. Get latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW .

articles.title: PGA Tour not planning return program for LIV Golf stars
articles.summary: PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp says there are no plans to create an instant pathway back for LIV Golf's biggest stars after the breakaway series filed for bankruptcy protection.
articles.body:
There are no plans to create an instant pathway back to the PGA Tour for LIV Golf's biggest stars.

Major winners Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith are contemplating their futures after LIV filed for bankruptcy protection last week as the breakaway league tries to create a new circuit for next year.

Rahm said he was uncertain about his future plans.

"There's a long legal process they have to go through before a lot of things fall into place," the Spaniard said before playing this week's BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.

"I really can't give you an answer right now."

The PGA Tour is pressing ahead with its plans for a revamped set-up in 2028 but chief executive Brian Rolapp offered no guarantees that LIV's biggest names will be welcomed back.

"In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning member program like the one you saw in January," Rolapp said.

Brooks Koepka took a deal that brought him back to the US tour at the start of the year but the arrangement was rejected by DeChambeau, Rahm and Smith.

LIV files for bankruptcy protection with over $45m owed to players

What next for LIV Golf's star players, and its fight for survival?

If players abandon LIV, it was thought their most likely route back to the PGA Tour would be through playing the DP World Tour.

Currently, the leading 10 finishers on the Race to Dubai earn cards for the American circuit, but that may change.

Rolapp admitted no deal has been struck over how many DP World Tour players will qualify for his circuit when it splits into a promotion and relegation setup with Championship and Challenger tiers from 2028.

Golfers who defected to LIV were hit with one-year bans that could be served while playing on the DP World Tour. Now it seems there are no guarantees as the revamping of the game's leading circuit continues.

"The PGA Tour is built on meritocracy," Rolapp said. "Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place.

"We are a membership organisation; we have rules, and those rules exist for lots of reasons, including fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter, and they must be enforced."

Rolapp added: "Accountability and discipline, these are essential elements for any sports league and are certainly for the integrity of the PGA Tour and the sport. It's what holds the tour together.

Negotiations with the DP World Tour over how many players will progress from the European based organisation to the PGA Tour are still to be concluded and the number of cards could be reduced.

"That's very much under discussion both internally and as we continue our discussions with the DP World Tour," Rolapp said.

"The spirit of those conversations are very productive. Both sides are trying to think creatively about how we modify and improve the relationship we have.

"Like any discussions, there's things we agree on, things we don't agree on, things we're trying to work through, and we'll continue to do that."

Rory McIIroy says he is not worried that a deal with the DP World Tour has yet to be concluded, but he warned that cards being made available for the lower Challenger Series would be less attractive.

"I don't see any reason why a DP World Tour player would go to the Challenger Series," said the two-time Masters champion. "I don't see that as an upward move in your career. I see it as a very lateral move."

McIlroy added: "No one's going to argue that the Championship Series is going to be the highest level of tour golf that you can play, and then it's just deciding what an adequate number of cards is to go from here to the Championship Series."

articles.title: Tiger Woods, más cerca de su regreso
articles.standfirst: El Tigre imparte un clínic durante la Nexus Cup en Nueva York y muestra su mejoría en el campo de prácticas
articles.summary: El Tigre imparte un clínic durante la Nexus Cup en Nueva York y muestra su mejoría en el campo de prácticas
articles.body: Tiger Woods ha estado alejado de la vida pública desde el accidente automovilístico que sufrió en marzo, pero esta semana podría participar en algún partido de la Nexus Cup en Nueva York, evento donde está involucrado benéficamente. Hoy se ha visto al californiano golpeando bolas en el campo de práctica en el Liberty National Golf Club. Durante el clínic que impartió, al Tigre le preguntaron cómo está progresando su juego, y este respondió: “Puedo golpear prácticamente cualquier cosa”. Sí que se pudo apreciar un swing muy limpio. Recordemos que Tiger no ha disputado una ronda competitiva desde el British Open de 2024 en Royal Troon, hace más de dos años. El 11 marzo de 2025 fue operado tras romperse el tendón de Aquiles izquierdo y en octubre de ese mismo año se sometió a su séptima intervención de espalda para reemplazar un disco en la parte baja. Se planteó su regreso en el pasado Masters, hasta que se vio involucrado en un accidente que le ha costado cinco años de retirada del carnet de conducir. El golfista se declaró culpable de conducción temeraria y de su negativa a someterse a una prueba legal después del incidente. Cabe recordar que antes de zanjar su caso con la Justicia estadounidense, Woods permaneció tres meses en un centro de rehabilitación en Suiza. Recientemente se habló de la posible participación del ganador de 15 Majors en el Baycurrent Classic (8 al 11 de octubre), un evento del PGA Tour que se celebra en Japón. Su figura aparece en el cartel promocional, pero él no ha confirmado absolutamente nada relacionado con su posible regreso a la competición.

articles.title: Where CBS Sports sees Florida playing its bowl game after Week 2
articles.summary: CBS Sports' college football bowl predictions have the Florida Gators heading to an in-state venue to take on Jon Sumrall's old team.
articles.body:
Following Florida football's Week 2 victory over the Campbell Fighting Camels at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, CBS Sports writer Chip Patterson has a new bowl game destination and opponent for the Orange and Blue.

Patterson now has the Gators facing Jon Sumrall's old team, the Tulane Green Wave , in the Gasparilla Bowl, which takes place in Tampa, Florida, on Dec. 18. It would be the third time in the program's last three postseason appearances that it played in the in-state event.

The last time the Gators played in the Gasparilla Bowl was in 2024, when Sumrall was in his first season at the helm of the Green Wave. His team fell to the Billy Napier-led Gators, 33-8, due to strong performances from quarterback DJ Lagway and running back Jadan Baugh.

Florida lost its only other Gasparilla Bowl matchup — a 29-17 loss to the UCF Knights in 2021 — in the final season of the Dan Mullen era. Greg Knox served as interim head coach after Mullen was dismissed with one game remaining on the regular-season schedule and Emory Jones played at quarterback despite already announcing his transfer portal intentions.

The Gators and Green Wave have met 22 times before on the collegiate gridiron, with Florida leading the all-time series with a 14-6-2 record. The last time Tulane prevailed was all the way back in 1946; UF finished 0-9 that season.

Patterson had previously projected Florida to take on the NC State Wolfpack in the Birmingham Bowl after Week 1.

articles.title: Mickelson’s Hidden Stake Vanishes in LIV Bankruptcy Filing
articles.summary: Phil Mickelson owns a piece of the golf league that is now on life support. Court records show the six-time major champion held a 0.23% stake in LIV Golf whe...
articles.body:
Phil Mickelson owns a piece of the golf league that is now on life support. Court records show the six-time major champion held a 0.23% stake in LIV Golf when the tour filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. This tiny slice of equity could vanish completely as the league attempts to restructure its massive debts. The move signals a grim reality for a player who once thought he was buying into a permanent empire.

The financial picture is bleak. Sportico reports the league held assets of $100 million to $500 million while facing liabilities between $500 million and $1 billion. That gap is too wide to bridge without major concessions. Court records indicate that on September 8th, LIV Golf and its related entities voluntarily sought Chapter 11 protection in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court of New Jersey. The Saudi Public Investment Fund, the primary backer, is walking away. Their equity and debt would be "canceled and extinguished in exchange for releases with no economic distribution on account of such debt and equity," per the proposed term sheet.

Mickelson is not the only one facing a dry spell. Top players like Jon Rahm are owed millions, with the league owing $7.5 million to Rahm and $5.7 million to Bryson DeChambeau, per reports. The proposed deal with private equity firm BC Partners aims to turn players into owners, but that only works if the players agree to take equity instead of cash. "This is very much not a done deal," Harvard law professor Jared A. Ellias said regarding the player buy-in requirement.

Mickelson's path back to the PGA Tour is gone. He missed all four major tournaments in 2026, a first in his career, citing family health matters. His reputation took another hit after allegations of inappropriate conduct surfaced at a San Diego club. A spokesperson said, "Any misunderstanding has been cleared up," but the damage remains.

Former ESPN anchor Trey Wingo was blunt about Mickelson's standing with the Tour. "And I can promise you one person that you'll never see in any way in an official capacity with the PGA Tour is Phil Mickelson," Wingo told Awful Announcing. "That bridge has been burned, detonated, destroyed, nuked, lasered to death."

The 56-year-old's $200 million guarantee from the 2022 launch is now part of a complex legal mess. He was the only "current player" listed as a shareholder in the filing documents. Now that the league is in court, his ownership stake is just another unsecured debt waiting to be resolved. Mickelson returned to LIV in 2026 but only played one event in South Africa. He has been largely silent on his future.

Scott O'Neil, the CEO, claims the league is entering a "next phase" designed to build a stronger future. But with the primary investor gone and debts piling up, the players hold the real power. Whether LIV Golf survives depends entirely on if the players want to keep playing for a company that cannot pay them. Whether Mickelson joins this "next phase" of LIV Golf or loses his share alongside the remaining debt remains to be seen over time.
